script: Neighbor was stealing water from my supply, so I ruined him.. Part 1: I bought a house in the capital, a fixer‑upper that had been left in the middle of a renovation. The previous owners were family friends who needed cash fast and had been living abroad for three years. I snagged it for a killer price. But here's the thing— the house had no gate, just a padlocked main door and a cracked garage door that any bike could ride into. What I didn't know was that the first day I moved in, a stranger parked his bike in the garage. I parked mine on the street, then put a gate up. An angry guy later knocked on my gate, but I ignored him. Through the window I saw him give up and take the bike after 15 minutes. The neighborhood felt sketchy, but I shrugged. No one ever bothered me again, except for random folks who didn't realize the house was no longer abandoned. I hung a "No Parking" sign, and the gate stayed shut most of the time. Last week, while showering, I noticed my water pressure was lower than usual. I heard a neighbor's water pump whirring. He was an old guy living on the lowest floor of a three‑story house; the other two floors were rented out. But here's the thing— he'd been vocal about how the sale bothered him, shouting at my friends, who warned me. I am a 6ft guy with three dogs, not a hero, but I didn't think he'd do anything. I was still on that same day when the water pump kicked on. I could hear it, and the pressure dropped again. I waited until it turned off, then checked the taps. The pressure was fine. What I didn't know was that the pump was a sign of water siphoning. The public supply's pressure wasn't enough to lift water up three stories, so the neighbor ran a pump to fill rooftop tanks. If the pump was running constantly, it meant something was wrong. I did the math: water bills had been climbing, the house had leaks, but the increase was too big for leaks alone. The old man was probably siphoning water from my mains. So I sat on it for a few days, thinking if I should confront him or go legal. Water in this country is cheap—my bill was like $5 a month with three dogs, a car, and a garden. But here's the thing— this wasn't about the money. It was about an entitled old guy stealing resources and getting away with it. The stakes were high: if I let it slide, he'd keep draining my water, and I'd lose control over my own supply. I'd have to pay for the damage, and the neighbor could blame me for any leaks. I decided to strike back without a fight. I'd turn off my water from the mains, and that's how I'd ruin his pump. I wouldn't break into his property or break the law—just a simple tap. But here's the thing— the way the tanks work, a ball valve detects the water level and sends a signal to the pump. If the level doesn't rise, the valve stays open, and the pump stays on until the level drops. What I didn't know was that a constantly running pump would overload the neighbor's 90s wiring, potentially causing a fire or blowing fuses. I set my plan in motion on Monday, four days ago. I waited until his pump flicked on, then turned off the supply. The pump tried to run, but no water came. The motor spun and spun, burning out the wiring. The neighbor's tenants woke up at 3 am, confused by a lack of water and power. They started shouting at their landlord, who had no idea why the house had no utilities. This is where it gets juicy. If the landlord had kept the house updated, he'd have avoided a fine and the loss of tenants. But he didn't. The tenants filed a complaint with the police, and the landlord faced a $500 fine. And that's when everything changed. The old guy's world crumbled— he lost his tenants, his income, and his pride. He'd have to move in with his daughter. The moment I turned off the tap, I felt like I'd just set the stage for a showdown. I didn't even know I'd set the stage for a showdown.
